extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on organizing material and composing effective news leads and bodies for newspaper stories, aimed at reporters preparing copy for the city desk. Covers note organization, story organization orders, lead types, and clarity/accuracy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize notes before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter should rearrange and order jumbled notes preparatory to composing the story rather than attempting to write straight from scattered, confusing pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizing aids speed, accuracy, and expression: reduces cognitive load so more attention can be given to composing forceful, accurate sentences; prevents inclusion of irrelevant facts and omission of illegible but important items. The wise reporter will have a definite plan for the story—mentally or on paper—before beginning to write; if rushed, be prepared to telephone facts to a rewrite man but do not idle away the return trip.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order notes to improve accuracy of statement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reorganization of notes before writing will aid accuracy of statement and presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because composing from jumbled notes consumes mental power needed for clear expression, reordering reduces the risk of including extraneous facts or omitting important items. Take time to group and interpret recorded facts so sentences can be accurate and vivid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select details to create a coherent angle and reader interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The reporter must select and arrange details with a definite point or 'angle' (the story's raison d'etre) determined by the paper's policy and readers' interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different selections/arrangements of the same facts can make a story humorous, pathetic, or prosaic. Reporter must choose details purposefully to produce specific appeal; without premeditated selection the narrative will be prosaic and less engaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use one of four orders of organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories may be organized in time order, space order, climactic order, or complex order, or combinations of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approximately 95% of news stories use time order (or a combination). Other orders are less common: climactic (~4%), space and complex (~1%). Reporters should know all four and apply the one best suited to the incident and desired effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time order (chronological arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange incidents in simple chronological sequence (time order).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most normal news stories follow time order; example provided (boy burned toes) shows simple sequential narration of events. Use when events are best understood by following the sequence in which they occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Space order (descriptive arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange material by physical or spatial relationships—descriptive writing that guides the reader through a scene or location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful to describe rooms, wreckage, inventories, or scenes (illustrated by Eastland disaster property inventory). Emphasize visible layout, objects, and sensory details to give descriptive completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climactic order (withhold outcome until ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange incidents so the reader does not know the outcome until the last sentences—like a short story climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective but difficult; beginners should generally avoid it. Useful sparingly in feature-like pieces. Some papers admit climactic stories rarely; reporter should learn technique but use cautiously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex order (from known to unknown; exposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceed from the known to the unknown—expository arrangement that increases complication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often used for explanatory news (e.g., patent/technical descriptions). Treat as straightforward exposition; useful when the reader needs background before novel information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place most important details first (inverted-pyramid principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the most important details at the beginning of the story and the least important last.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers want the main details immediately to judge interest; early editions are often cut for later editions, so the story should be written so that the end can be pruned without losing the gist. If editor trims to the first paragraph, the reader should still get what happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write so story can be cut from the tail
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan the story with the expectation that later parts may be cut; structure so pruning leaves a complete gist in early paragraphs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because later editions accumulate more important news and space is limited, reporters should arrange so the last parts are least essential and may be removed without destroying the core of the story. Example: a multi-paragraph piece that can be cut after any paragraph and still present a coherent account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present facts with judicial impartiality (accuracy of presentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When arranging material, reporters must present facts impartially and avoid warping narrative by unfair arrangement or suppression of facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A newspaper reporter has no right to willfully keep back information or distort news. While legitimate to order topics for effect (humor, pathos, etc.), desire for effect must never distort facts. Suppression of a single fact can woefully distort a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult the city editor before writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Before beginning the story, report briefly to the city editor, summarize findings, and ask for instructions about handling or features to play up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The city editor may give no guidance, may request a particular feature or tone, or suggest multiple possible angles; experienced reporters often bring two or three leads to give the editor options. The city editor often takes cues from the reporter's presentation; prepare to adapt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know two kinds of leads: summarizing and informal
rubrics_metrics.description: The lead (first sentence/group of sentences) is of two kinds: the summarizing lead, which gives the gist in concise language, and the informal lead, which introduces the story without revealing the outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The summarizing lead is far more common and can be one sentence or a paragraph (or several paragraphs for complex stories). Informal leads suggest something interesting is coming but don't summarize the outcome; use when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead should answer who, what, when, where, why, how
rubrics_metrics.description: The first commandment in news writing is that the story begin with the most important fact and give all essential details, generally summarized by who, what, when, where, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the lead answers these questions, it will be contextually sound. Determine which of these details will be most interesting to your readers and play them up in the lead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature the most newsworthy aspect in the lead (result/cause/means/name/place/time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide what feature to play up in the lead—commonly result, cause, means/method, name, place, or time—and make that the opening emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: result-focused leads (outcome of an action), cause-focused leads (motive), means (method by which result was attained), names when notable persons are central, place and time where occasional emphasis is warranted. Choose the element most likely to interest readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid beginning leads with trivial elements (time/article/place) when not important
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid starting with 'to-day', 'to-morrow', 'the', or place name unless those are the most important features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Time or place rarely merits first position unless it's key; begin with the result or cause for greater impact. Use articles at start only when the noun they modify is itself important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate grammatical form for the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Common grammatical beginnings include simple statement, series of simple statements, conditional clause, substantive clause, infinitive phrase, participial phrase, prepositional phrase, and the absolute construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select form based on purpose: short sentences lend force; conditional clauses can be humorous or useful for summarizing lead-in facts but avoid using more than two as they can become heavy; participial phrases must have definite words to modify; absolute constructions are forceful but unwieldy—avoid for beginners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short sentences in leads for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking a lead into very short sentences or a series of short sentences can lend force and emphasis to individual details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short-sentence leads make each important detail stand out; examples show a short headline-like sentence followed by a one- or two-sentence elaboration. Use this for brevity and punch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with conditional-clause leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Leads beginning with conditional clauses can be valuable for humor or for summarizing lead-up facts but should be limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid more than two conditional clauses in a lead because multiple conditionals can make the sentence heavy or obscure the meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure participial and phrase leads clearly modify words
rubrics_metrics.description: When beginning a lead with infinitive, participial, or prepositional phrases, ensure the phrase has a clear and definite word to modify to avoid ambiguity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases are useful for emphasis but misattachment can make the sentence confusing. Check that modifiers have clear antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overloaded leads; prefer cutting into short, crisp sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not crowd the lead with too many details; overloaded leads risk being misunderstood and turning readers away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lead is overloaded, cut it into two or more short sentences. Examples show a long, tangled sentence improved by splitting into a brief, clear lead followed by supporting sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead must have both accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Two requirements for any lead are accuracy (truth) and interest (ability to lure the reader to the story).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy is for truth; interest is to attract readership. Organizing material and selecting facts should aim to maximize both. A clearly organized and honest lead best achieves these.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain clearness in the lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard against any construction or detail that blurs absolute clarity of the lead; if a reader cannot grasp the lead readily, they will likely not read the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid obscure constructions, overloaded sentences, and awkward phrasing. Improve clarity by simplifying, splitting sentences, and ensuring logical arrangement of details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use boxed summaries for very long or complicated stories
rubrics_metrics.description: For unusually long and complicated stories, prepare a boxed digest (summary) of principal items to display before the regular lead when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boxed summaries are usually determined by the city editor or copy readers but suggesting a boxed summary can be helpful. Common types: accident lists (dead/injured), athletic event summaries, speeches/trials/executions (notable quotations), diplomatic letters (main points), lengthy reports. Prepare a separate grouping of outstanding facts for the city editor if unsure.
